cai-troi-luoc-cham-mam-cai-phu-yen.name: Phu Yen Boiled Cai Troi Greens with Fermented Fish Sauce
aliases: Boiled cai troi with mam cai
Phu Yen wild greens with fermented fish dip
cai-troi-luoc-cham-mam-cai-phu-yen.serving_basis: One shared side dish of greens for four people; seasonal wild greens shrink considerably when boiled.
cai-troi-luoc-cham-mam-cai-phu-yen.description: Cai troi grows around the hills and fields of Phu Yen. Local accounts describe briefly boiling the greens and dipping them in mam cai, a fermented fish sauce. Bep Viet standardizes the washing and four-person quantities while keeping the quick-cooking method so the greens retain their delicate aroma.
cai-troi-luoc-cham-mam-cai-phu-yen.finished_dish: Just-tender greens with soft-crisp stems and deep green leaves, served beside a fragrant, savory bowl of mam cai with optional fresh chili.
cai-troi-luoc-cham-mam-cai-phu-yen.serving: Drain the greens and arrange them on a plate. Serve warm or just cooled with a separate bowl of mam cai and steamed rice.
tips: Use cai troi only when its identity is confirmed by a trusted seller or knowledgeable forager; do not eat unidentified wild plants.
Wash several times, especially around the roots and leaf folds, to remove grit.
Add the greens to vigorously boiling water and remove as soon as tender; prolonged cooking dulls their characteristic aroma.
Taste the mam cai before adding anything because its saltiness and texture vary by maker.
cai-troi-luoc-cham-mam-cai-phu-yen.image_alt: A plate of freshly boiled Phu Yen cai troi greens beside a small bowl of mam cai with red chili.
cai-troi-luoc-cham-mam-cai-phu-yen.time_note: About 20 minutes; washing and picking time depends on how tender and sandy the greens are.

ingredients.name: Young cai troi greens
ingredients.notes: Choose tender, undamaged greens; weigh after removing tough roots.

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: Enough to submerge the greens in a wide pot.

ingredients.name: Coarse salt
ingredients.notes: Optional in the blanching water.

ingredients.name: Mam cai fermented fish sauce
ingredients.notes: Serve separately for dipping; choose a style suited to the household.

ingredients.name: Fresh chili
ingredients.notes: Slice and serve with the fermented fish sauce if desired.

preparation_steps: Remove tough roots and wilted leaves. Wash the greens several times, briefly soak in clean water, rinse again and drain.
Bring a wide pot of water to the boil. Spoon the mam cai into a small bowl and slice the chili if using.
cooking_steps: Bring the water to a vigorous boil and add the coarse salt if desired. Cook the greens in batches sized for the pot.
Add the greens and turn gently to submerge them. As soon as the water returns to a boil and the stems are tender, lift them into a colander.
Let the greens drain naturally, arrange on a plate and serve with mam cai; add sliced chili to the dip to taste.

rau-chua-le-luoc-phu-yen.name: Quick-Boiled Chua Le Greens from Phu Yen
rau-chua-le-luoc-phu-yen.serving_basis: One seasonal plate of greens for four people; the small leaves shrink substantially when cooked.
rau-chua-le-luoc-phu-yen.description: Chua le is a seasonal wild green gathered around the hills of Phu Yen during the rainy season. Local cooks add it to already-boiling water and lift it out as soon as the water comes back to a boil, preserving the stems' crisp texture and mild tartness. Bep Viet edits the household quantity for four and does not assign a regional dipping sauce that the source does not document.
rau-chua-le-luoc-phu-yen.finished_dish: Barely tender leaves and fine stems that remain pleasantly crisp, with a light natural sourness.
rau-chua-le-luoc-phu-yen.serving: Drain well and serve as a vegetable side with rice. A familiar household dipping sauce may be served separately if desired.
tips: Use only greens positively identified by a knowledgeable seller or forager and collected away from sprayed areas; never eat unidentified wild plants.
Soak briefly so grit settles, then rinse gently several times because the greens grow close to the ground.
Boil small handfuls in vigorously boiling water and lift them out as soon as the water returns to a boil.
The small greens lose considerable volume; prepare more raw greens than for a typical side dish.
rau-chua-le-luoc-phu-yen.image_alt: A plate of tender, quickly boiled chua le greens from Phu Yen, with fine stems and intact leaves.
rau-chua-le-luoc-phu-yen.time_note: About 18 minutes; picking can take longer because the greens are small and often gritty.

ingredients.name: Young chua le greens
ingredients.notes: Select tender shoots; cooked yield is much lower than the raw weight.

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: Use a wide pot so the greens return to the boil quickly.

ingredients.name: Coarse salt
ingredients.notes: Optional; keep the greens lightly seasoned.

preparation_steps: Remove tough, damaged or mixed-in plants. Soak briefly in clean water so grit settles, then rinse gently several times.
Bring a large pot of water to a vigorous boil and set a clean colander nearby so the greens can be lifted out promptly.
cooking_steps: Add one handful of greens to the boiling water and gently press them under with chopsticks.
Watch closely and lift them out immediately when the water returns to a boil. Repeat with the remaining greens to keep the pot hot.
Drain naturally without soaking in cold water; this preserves the stems' crispness and mild tartness. Serve with the meal.

rau-bo-may-luoc-muoi-vung-thai-nguyen.name: Thai Nguyen Boiled Bo May Greens with Sesame Salt
aliases: Thai Nguyen dang cay greens with sesame salt
rau-bo-may-luoc-muoi-vung-thai-nguyen.serving_basis: One shared plate of young greens and a small bowl of sesame salt for four people.
rau-bo-may-luoc-muoi-vung-thai-nguyen.description: Bo may, also called dang cay, is remembered in Thai Nguyen as a seasonal wild green with a pleasantly bitter taste. Local reporting describes boiling the young shoots and leaves and eating them with sesame salt. Bep Viet edits a practical four-person home preparation while retaining this documented pairing.
rau-bo-may-luoc-muoi-vung-thai-nguyen.finished_dish: Tender, vivid greens with a gentle bitter edge, paired with nutty toasted sesame crushed with salt.
rau-bo-may-luoc-muoi-vung-thai-nguyen.serving: Drain the greens and place them on a shared plate. Serve with a small bowl of freshly crushed sesame salt and steamed rice.
tips: Buy bo may from a trusted local source that can identify it; do not substitute an unidentified wild plant.
Use young shoots and leaves, which cook quickly and have a more tender texture.
Toast sesame over low heat until aromatic, then cool before crushing so it stays nutty rather than scorched.
Keep the sesame salt lightly seasoned so the greens' characteristic bitterness remains noticeable.
rau-bo-may-luoc-muoi-vung-thai-nguyen.image_alt: Young boiled bo may greens with a small bowl of freshly crushed toasted sesame salt.
rau-bo-may-luoc-muoi-vung-thai-nguyen.time_note: About 22 minutes, including picking, washing and preparing the sesame salt.

ingredients.name: Young bo may greens
ingredients.notes: Use a trusted source; select young leaves and shoots only.

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: Enough to cover the greens in a wide pot.

ingredients.name: Coarse salt for blanching
ingredients.notes: Optional; reduce or omit to taste.

ingredients.name: White sesame seeds
ingredients.notes: Toast over low heat until fragrant; cool before crushing.

ingredients.name: Salt for sesame dip
ingredients.notes: Crush with the sesame and season lightly.

preparation_steps: Pick the young shoots and leaves; discard tough or damaged portions. Wash several times and drain.
Toast the sesame in a dry pan over low heat until fragrant and lightly golden. Cool, then crush coarsely with salt.
cooking_steps: Bring a pot of water to a vigorous boil; add a little salt if desired.
Add the greens, turn to submerge and boil for about 2–4 minutes depending on stem thickness. Lift them out as soon as tender.
Drain, arrange on a plate and serve with the crushed sesame salt.

mang-ngot-luoc-cham-cham-cheo-dien-bien.name: Dien Bien Sweet Bamboo Shoots with Cham Cheo
aliases: Boiled sweet bamboo shoots with cham cheo
mang-ngot-luoc-cham-cham-cheo-dien-bien.serving_basis: One shared plate of boiled bamboo shoots with a small bowl of fresh cham cheo for four people.
mang-ngot-luoc-cham-cham-cheo-dien-bien.description: Boiled sweet bamboo shoots are part of Thai home meals in the Northwest and are served with fresh cham cheo. Regional reporting describes the dip with salt, chili, garlic, aromatic herbs and either mac khen or doi seed. Bep Viet sets home quantities and a safe boiling method; the dip ratio is an editorial adaptation, not a single canonical recipe.
mang-ngot-luoc-cham-cham-cheo-dien-bien.finished_dish: Tender ivory bamboo shoots with a mild sweetness, served beside a rustic, fragrant, spicy-salty cham cheo with fresh herbs.
mang-ngot-luoc-cham-cham-cheo-dien-bien.serving: Drain the shoots and arrange on a plate. Serve cham cheo in a separate bowl for dipping while the shoots are warm.
tips: Choose fresh, sweet bamboo shoots from a reliable seller and remove all tough outer sheaths.
Bamboo shoots must be thoroughly cooked; if they remain bitter or pungent, change the water and continue boiling.
Toast mac khen briefly over low heat before crushing to release its aroma; use either mac khen or doi seed, not both unless desired.
Add the herbs after crushing the salt, chili, garlic and spice so their fresh fragrance remains.
mang-ngot-luoc-cham-cham-cheo-dien-bien.image_alt: Tender boiled sweet bamboo shoots beside a fresh cham cheo dip with chili, garlic, mac khen and herbs.
mang-ngot-luoc-cham-cham-cheo-dien-bien.time_note: About 50 minutes; thicker or more pungent shoots may need longer boiling or a change of water.

ingredients.name: Fresh sweet bamboo shoots
ingredients.notes: Remove old sheaths, wash well and cut into serving pieces.

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: Enough to cover the bamboo shoots in the pot.

ingredients.name: Salt for boiling
ingredients.notes: Optional; omit if the cham cheo is sufficiently seasoned.

ingredients.name: Coarse salt for cham cheo
ingredients.notes: Crush into the fresh dipping sauce.

ingredients.name: Fresh chili
ingredients.notes: Lightly roast or use fresh; adjust to taste.

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.notes: Peel and crush with the salt and chili.

ingredients.name: Toasted mac khen
ingredients.notes: Toast and crush; doi seed may be used instead.

ingredients.name: Cilantro
ingredients.notes: Wash, drain and chop.

ingredients.name: Culantro
ingredients.notes: Wash, drain and chop; aromatic mint can be substituted.

preparation_steps: Remove old sheaths and the fibrous base from the bamboo shoots. Wash thoroughly and cut into slices or bite-size pieces.
Wash and drain the cilantro and culantro, then chop. Toast the mac khen in a dry pan until fragrant.
In a clean mortar, crush the salt, chili, garlic and mac khen; add the herbs last.
cooking_steps: Cover the bamboo shoots with cold water, bring to a boil and simmer for about 25–35 minutes or until tender. If they remain pungent, replace the water and continue boiling.
Crush the salt, chili, garlic and mac khen into a coarse mixture. Add the herbs and crush briefly to combine.
Drain the shoots, arrange on a plate and serve with the fresh cham cheo.

ngon-dau-den-luoc-cham-nuoc-mam-toi.name: Boiled Black Bean Shoots with Garlic Fish Sauce
aliases: Young bean shoots with garlic fish sauce
ngon-dau-den-luoc-cham-nuoc-mam-toi.serving_basis: One shared plate of young black bean shoots with a bowl of dipping sauce for four people.
ngon-dau-den-luoc-cham-nuoc-mam-toi.description: Young black bean shoots are a thrifty home vegetable: the tender tips removed while growing beans can be boiled and dipped in tangy, spicy garlic fish sauce. Dak Lak reporting describes their nutty-sweet flavor and this simple preparation. Bep Viet edits the four-person quantities and balances the dip to household taste without assigning the dish to a specific province.
ngon-dau-den-luoc-cham-nuoc-mam-toi.finished_dish: Soft, tender leaves and stems with a mild nutty sweetness, paired with a balanced, garlicky, lightly sour and spicy fish sauce.
ngon-dau-den-luoc-cham-nuoc-mam-toi.serving: Drain the shoots well and serve on a plate with a separate bowl of garlic fish sauce and hot rice.
tips: Buy shoots positively identified as black bean from a trusted grower; do not use leaves from unfamiliar bean plants.
Wash gently and remove tough stems without bruising the leaves.
Boil only until the stems are tender, then drain promptly to avoid limp, discolored greens.
Mix the fish sauce separately and season gradually so it complements rather than overwhelms the beans' mild flavor.
search_terms: bean shoots with garlic fish sauce
ngon-dau-den-luoc-cham-nuoc-mam-toi.image_alt: Young boiled black bean shoots arranged on a plate beside a small bowl of garlic chili fish sauce.
ngon-dau-den-luoc-cham-nuoc-mam-toi.time_note: About 18 minutes; picking takes longer when the shoots include many tough stems.

ingredients.name: Young black bean shoots
ingredients.notes: Keep tender leaves and stems; discard tough sections.

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: Enough to submerge the shoots in a wide pot.

ingredients.name: Coarse salt
ingredients.notes: Optional in the blanching water.

ingredients.name: Fish sauce
ingredients.notes: Use for the dipping sauce.

ingredients.name: Lime juice
ingredients.notes: Add a light sour note and adjust to taste.

ingredients.name: Sugar
ingredients.notes: Balances the salt without making the dip sweet.

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.notes: Peel and finely mince.

ingredients.name: Fresh chili
ingredients.notes: Mince and add optionally.

ingredients.name: Warm water
ingredients.notes: Dilutes the fish sauce and dissolves the sugar.

preparation_steps: Pick through the shoots and remove tough or damaged stems. Rinse gently several times and drain.
Mince the garlic and chili. Stir the fish sauce, warm water, sugar and lime juice until dissolved, then add the garlic and chili.
cooking_steps: Bring a wide pot of water to a vigorous boil and add salt if desired. Add the shoots and gently press them under.
Boil for about 3–5 minutes depending on tenderness. Check that the stems are just soft, then lift the shoots out to drain.
Arrange on a plate and serve with the sweet-sour garlic chili fish sauce and hot rice.
